content.title: Moya Brennan, 'First Lady of Celtic music', dies at 73
content.text: From Gaeltacht roots to world stages Born Máire Ní Bhraonáin in Gweedore, County Donegal, Moya Brennan was the eldest of nine children in a renowned musical family. She formed Clannad in 1970 with her brothers and uncles, later joined briefly by her sister Enya, blending traditional Irish music with contemporary influences. Their early performances in the family pub evolved into a global career marked by millions of album sales and international tours. The Independent + 3 Breakthrough with Harry’s Game Clannad’s 1982 theme for ITV’s 'Harry’s Game' became a UK chart hit and the first Irish-language song performed on Top of the Pops. The haunting track won an Ivor Novello Award and was later featured in films and advertising, cementing the band’s international profile. This success paved the way for further accolades, including a BAFTA for 'Robin of Sherwood' and a Grammy for 'Landmarks'. The Independent + 3 Tributes honour a cultural ambassador Taoiseach Micheál Martin, Tánaiste Simon Harris, and Sinn Féin TD Pearse Doherty hailed Brennan as an 'iconic Irish voice' and 'First Lady of Celtic music'. Musicians including Frances Black, Una Healy, and Daniel O’Donnell praised her generosity, spirituality, and the global reach of her artistry. Many highlighted her role in promoting Irish culture, language, and music to audiences far beyond Ireland. Derry Journal + 3 "Along with her Clannad bandmates, Moya brought Irish folk music to the international stage. Deepest sympathies to Moya’s family and friends at this difficult time. Ar dheis Dé go raibh a hanam."Micheál Martin Enduring legacy in music and culture Over her career, Brennan recorded more than 30 albums with Clannad and as a solo artist, selling over 20 million records. She collaborated with artists like Bono and Hans Zimmer, contributed to major film soundtracks, and remained active despite her 2020 pulmonary fibrosis diagnosis. Her work has left a lasting imprint on Celtic music, inspiring future generations to embrace and share Ireland’s cultural heritage. The Independent + 4 8 references
